Lactulose

Lactulose is a non absorbable synthetic disaccharide made of galactose and fructose

Lactulose can’t be metabolized in the small intestine so it reaches the large intestine unchanged and that is where it get metabolized by the colonic bacteria to monosaccharides and then to fatty acids, hydrogen and methane

Yikrazuul, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

Monosaccharides in the colon act as an osmolyte that draws water out of the colon wall (osmotic effect) and it also lead to increased gas formation (methane) => more water and gas in the colon lead to laxative effect => reduction in transit time => treatment of constipation (it is classified as osmotic laxative)

By this mechanism, lactulose work to treat constipation and it is FDA approved for this indication

Breakdown of lactulose to short chain fatty acids (e.g. lactic acid and acetic acid) lead to Reduction in PH which facilitates conversion of ammonia NH3 into ammonium NH4+ in the large intestine

Ammonium NH4+ would not diffuse to bloodstream as much as ammonia NH3 diffuses due to its charge; also it can’t cross BBB for the same reason

The acidic PH also work to destroy urease producing bacteria involved in the production of ammonia => less ammonia produced

Also, lactulose inhibit intestinal glutaminase activity which blocks the conversion of glutamate to glutamine and its metabolism to ammonia

By these 3 mechanisms, lactulose work to lower blood ammonia and treat hepatic encephalopathy and that is also an FDA approved therapeutic use for this medication

Therapeutic uses

FDA approved therapeutic uses

Prevention and treatment of hepatic encephalopathy, lactulose decreases blood ammonia levels by 25% to 50% and this improve patient mental state

Used as a third line in Management of chronic constipation (after lifestyle modifications and increasing fiber intake have failed)

Off label uses

Management of subacute clinical encephalopathy

Because of its ability to reduce intestinal transit time, lactulose can also reduce deoxycholic acid’s hypersaturation => leading to inhibition of cholesterol stone formation

Pharmacokinetics

Lactulose is available as syrup for oral administration and a rectal enema

Lactulose is poorly absorbed from GI tract and it work locally there

Less than 3% of the total dose is absorbed to the blood and excreted through urine

Adverse effects

Since lactulose doesn’t get absorbed into the blood, it produces side effects limited to the GI tract

The most significant side effect is diarrhea which is dose dependent and decreases in severity with dose reduction

Diarrhea may lead to electrolyte disturbances

It also may lead to increased bowel sounds, increased flatus, and sensation of bloating

Notes

Lactulose is contraindicated in galactosemia patients requiring galactose free diet

Sorbitol is superior in treatment of constipation in elderly patients

Lactulose may lead to electrolyte imbalances due to its osmotic effect, electrolyte might require monitoring especially in elderly and critically ill patients

Lactulose may induce lithium toxicity in psychiatry patients due to its ability to induce dehydration through its osmotic action leading to poor renal excretion of lithium
